subChunks.title: Subqueries — Queries Inside Queries
subChunks.hookHtml: Sometimes a single SELECT can't answer your question. "Apprentices whose XP exceeds the average" requires you to compute the average first, then filter against it. The answer is a subquery — a query nested inside another. Once you see the pattern, half of "hard SQL questions" become straightforward.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Three places a subquery can live

  1. In WHERE — to compare against a computed value
  2. In FROM — to use a query's result as if it were a table (a derived table)
  3. In SELECT — to compute a per-row value (a scalar subquery)

Subquery in WHERE — scalar comparison

-- Apprentices with above-average XP:
SELECT name, xp
FROM apprentices
WHERE xp > (SELECT AVG(xp) FROM apprentices);

The inner query returns a single number — the average. The outer query compares each apprentice's XP against that single number. Three apprentices, average = 2120, so Bjorn (2400) and Cassia (4800) come back.

Subquery in WHERE — list membership (IN)

-- Apprentices who have completed at least one quest with reward over 200:
SELECT name
FROM apprentices
WHERE id IN (
  SELECT apprentice_id
  FROM completions c
  JOIN quests q ON q.id = c.quest_id
  WHERE q.xp_reward > 200
);

The inner query returns a list of apprentice ids. The outer query filters to those.

This is one of two ways to express the same intent — the other is JOIN ... DISTINCT, or (we'll see in sql-e2) WHERE EXISTS. Different shapes, often equivalent results, occasionally different performance.

Subquery in FROM — derived table

-- Per-rank average XP, alongside the global average:
SELECT rank,
       avg_per_rank,
       (SELECT AVG(xp) FROM apprentices) AS global_avg
FROM (
  SELECT rank, AVG(xp) AS avg_per_rank
  FROM apprentices
  GROUP BY rank
) per_rank;

The derived table per_rank is computed first, then the outer query reads it as if it were a real table. Note the alias per_rank — derived tables require an alias in most engines.

Subquery in SELECT — scalar per-row

-- Each apprentice with their completion count:
SELECT a.name,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM completions c WHERE c.apprentice_id = a.id)
         AS num_completed
FROM apprentices a;

The subquery runs once per outer row, and depends on a.id from the outer scope — that makes it a correlated subquery (next sub-chunk). For the simple case here, an equivalent JOIN-and-GROUP-BY is usually faster:

SELECT a.name, COUNT(c.id) AS num_completed
FROM apprentices a
LEFT JOIN completions c ON c.apprentice_id = a.id
GROUP BY a.id, a.name;

Mental model — read inside-out

For a nested query, always read the innermost subquery first. Resolve it to a value (a number, a list, or a virtual table). Then walk outward, treating each subquery's result as a fact you already know. The query may be three levels deep on the page, but it's still a sequence of small clear steps in your head.

The most common subquery anti-pattern

-- Slow, hard to read:
SELECT a.name
FROM apprentices a
WHERE a.id IN (
  SELECT c.apprentice_id
  FROM completions c
);

-- Often clearer (and sometimes faster):
SELECT DISTINCT a.name
FROM apprentices a
JOIN completions c ON c.apprentice_id = a.id;

Both return the same names. The JOIN form makes the table relationships explicit. The subquery form is more concise. Performance depends on the engine and the indexes — modern optimisers usually rewrite one into the other anyway. Pick the one that reads more clearly for your query.

storyBeats.text: Cipher rolls a fresh sheet across the desk and writes a single phrase at the top: 'Above average.'

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: The Headmaster wants 'every apprentice whose XP is above the Academy's average.' This is a question that refers to itself. To answer it, I must first compute the average, and then filter using that value. One question, two queries — one nested inside the other.

storyBeats.speaker: Above average — a subquery in WHERE
storyBeats.text:
SELECT name, xp
FROM apprentices
WHERE xp > (SELECT AVG(xp) FROM apprentices);

-- Step 1: inner query computes one number — 2120.0
-- Step 2: outer query becomes:
--   SELECT name, xp FROM apprentices WHERE xp > 2120.0;
-- Result:
--   Bjorn  | 2400
--   Cassia | 4800

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Read it inside-out. Innermost first. Resolve the inner query to a value — here, the number 2120. Substitute that value where the subquery sits. The remaining outer query is something you already know how to read. This habit — read inside-out — handles every nested query you will ever meet, no matter how deep.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Three places a subquery can sit: WHERE (to compare against a computed value or list), FROM (to use the result as a table), and SELECT (to compute a value per outer row). Each is occasionally the right tool. Most beginners overuse WHERE ... IN (subquery) and underuse derived tables in FROM — which is often the cleaner expression.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Trace each subquery

For each query, identify what the inner subquery returns (number? list? table?), then resolve the outer query against that result.
subChunks.guidedPracticeStarterCode:
-- apprentices: Alice(1, 1200), Bjorn(2, 2400), Cassia(3, 4800), Dorian(4, 80)
-- quests:      1=Tame the Slime(100), 2=Decode the Glyph(180),
--              3=Forge the Blade(400)
-- completions: (app=1,q=1), (app=2,q=1), (app=2,q=2), (app=3,q=3)

-- Query A — above average XP:
SELECT name, xp
FROM apprentices
WHERE xp > (SELECT AVG(xp) FROM apprentices);

-- Query B — apprentices who completed any quest worth more than 150 XP:
SELECT name
FROM apprentices
WHERE id IN (
  SELECT c.apprentice_id
  FROM completions c
  JOIN quests q ON q.id = c.quest_id
  WHERE q.xp_reward > 150
);

-- Query C — derived table in FROM:
SELECT rank, mean_xp
FROM (
  SELECT rank, AVG(xp) AS mean_xp
  FROM apprentices
  GROUP BY rank
) per_rank
WHERE mean_xp > 1000;

-- Query D — scalar subquery in SELECT:
SELECT a.name,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM completions c WHERE c.apprentice_id = a.id)
         AS num_done
FROM apprentices a;
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Walk a junior through the query 'WHERE xp > (SELECT AVG(xp) FROM apprentices)' step by step. Then explain the difference between a scalar subquery (returns one value) and a list subquery (returns one column with many values), and where each is used.

options: A subquery that returns exactly one row, one column — i.e. a single value
A subquery that uses scalar functions like ABS or LOWER
Any subquery in the SELECT clause
A subquery without a WHERE clause
questions.correctAnswer: A subquery that returns exactly one row, one column — i.e. a single value
questions.explanationHtml: Scalar = single value. Scalar subqueries can sit anywhere a single value can — in WHERE comparisons, in SELECT projections, in CASE expressions. If a scalar subquery returns more than one row, the engine errors out (or, worse on some old engines, picks one arbitrarily).

questions.questionHtml:
Using the four-apprentice table from the lesson (XPs: 1200, 2400, 4800, 80; average = 2120), what does this query return?

SELECT name FROM apprentices
WHERE xp > (SELECT AVG(xp) FROM apprentices);
options: Bjorn, Cassia
Cassia
Alice, Bjorn, Cassia
Nothing
questions.explanationHtml: Inner query: AVG = (1200+2400+4800+80)/4 = 8480/4 = 2120. Outer: xp > 2120 → Bjorn (2400) and Cassia (4800). Alice (1200) and Dorian (80) are below average.

questions.questionHtml: Which clause does a list subquery (returning multiple values) commonly pair with?
options: WHERE col IN (...)
WHERE col = (...)
WHERE col HAS (...)
WHERE col CONTAINS (...)
questions.explanationHtml: IN (subquery) tests membership in the result list. WHERE col = (subquery) requires the subquery to return exactly one value (scalar) — passing it a list errors. HAS and CONTAINS are not standard SQL keywords.

questions.questionHtml:
Two queries claim to find "apprentices who have completed at least one quest." Which one is functionally equivalent and clearer?

-- Version A:
SELECT a.name FROM apprentices a
WHERE a.id IN (SELECT apprentice_id FROM completions);

-- Version B:
SELECT DISTINCT a.name FROM apprentices a
JOIN completions c ON c.apprentice_id = a.id;
options: Both return the same set of names; A is more concise, B makes the relationship explicit. Modern optimisers usually rewrite them to the same plan
A returns the names; B returns Cartesian-product duplicates without the DISTINCT
A is faster than B in every engine because it avoids the join entirely
B is required if any apprentice_id is NULL
questions.correctAnswer: Both return the same set of names; A is more concise, B makes the relationship explicit. Modern optimisers usually rewrite them to the same plan
questions.explanationHtml: Both express "apprentices with at least one match in completions." The optimiser typically transforms IN-subquery into a semi-join (the same physical operation as DISTINCT JOIN). Pick whichever reads clearer for the team and the query. Version B's DISTINCT is necessary because an apprentice with multiple completions would otherwise appear multiple times in the join result.

subChunks.title: Correlated Subqueries & EXISTS
subChunks.hookHtml: A regular subquery runs once and is done. A correlated subquery runs once per outer row, referring back to that row's columns. It's slower if used carelessly, but it's the natural shape of "for each apprentice, ask a question about their own data." Plus you'll meet EXISTS — the most efficient way to test "is there at least one match?"
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Regular vs correlated subqueries

-- REGULAR — inner runs once, outer reuses the result:
SELECT name FROM apprentices
WHERE xp > (SELECT AVG(xp) FROM apprentices);

-- CORRELATED — inner refers to the outer row (a.id),
-- so it re-runs once for each outer row:
SELECT a.name
FROM apprentices a
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM completions c
  WHERE c.apprentice_id = a.id     ← refers to outer 'a'
);

The give-away of a correlated subquery: the inner query references a column from the outer query.

EXISTS — "is there at least one matching row?"

-- Apprentices who have completed at least one quest:
SELECT a.name
FROM apprentices a
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM completions c
  WHERE c.apprentice_id = a.id
);

The SELECT 1 is convention — EXISTS doesn't care what columns the subquery returns, only whether any row matches. SELECT 1, SELECT *, SELECT NULL all work. SELECT 1 signals "I'm using EXISTS, the values don't matter."

NOT EXISTS — "is there no matching row?"

-- Apprentices who have completed NO quests:
SELECT a.name
FROM apprentices a
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM completions c
  WHERE c.apprentice_id = a.id
);

This is the third way to find orphans (the others being LEFT JOIN ... WHERE c.id IS NULL and WHERE id NOT IN (subquery)). All three return the same rows when the data is clean.

The NOT IN + NULL trap

This is one of the deepest SQL gotchas. NOT IN with a list that contains NULL silently returns nothing:

-- If completions.apprentice_id has any NULL, this returns no rows:
SELECT a.name FROM apprentices a
WHERE a.id NOT IN (SELECT apprentice_id FROM completions);

Why? x NOT IN (list) is equivalent to x <> v1 AND x <> v2 AND ... AND x <> NULL. The last AND-clause is NULL (any comparison with NULL produces NULL), and TRUE AND NULL = NULL, which is not TRUE — so no row passes.

The fix: use NOT EXISTS, which has correct NULL semantics. Or filter NULLs out of the inner query.

-- Safe — NOT EXISTS doesn't have the NULL problem:
SELECT a.name FROM apprentices a
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM completions c WHERE c.apprentice_id = a.id
);

EXISTS vs IN — performance

For small inner tables, both perform similarly. For large inner tables, EXISTS often wins because the engine can stop scanning as soon as it finds the first matching row per outer row — it only needs "yes/no," not the full list. IN historically required materialising the full list. Modern optimisers blur the difference, but EXISTS remains the safer default for "existence" questions, and IN for "membership in a known list."

The mental model

Picture a correlated subquery as a nested for-loop: for each outer row, run the inner query. EXISTS is the outer for-loop continuing as soon as the inner one finds anything. NOT EXISTS is the outer row passing only if the inner loop finds nothing.

// Pseudocode for: SELECT a.name FROM apprentices a WHERE EXISTS (...)
for (apprentice a in apprentices) {
  if (any row exists in completions where apprentice_id = a.id) {
    yield a.name;
  }
}

This explicit-loop picture makes correlated subqueries feel inevitable rather than weird.

storyBeats.text: Cipher draws a small loop on a corner of the parchment, then a smaller loop inside it.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Picture two nested loops. Outer loop: each apprentice. Inner loop: each completion. For each apprentice, ask 'is there any completion that belongs to me?' If yes, include the apprentice. If no, skip. That nested-loop picture is a correlated subquery. The inner query refers to the outer row — that's what makes it correlated.

storyBeats.speaker: EXISTS — the existence check
storyBeats.text:
-- Apprentices who have completed any quest:
SELECT a.name
FROM apprentices a
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM completions c
  WHERE c.apprentice_id = a.id
);

-- Mental model:
-- for each apprentice a:
--   if (any completion has apprentice_id = a.id):
--     yield a.name

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: And one nasty trap. WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT apprentice_id FROM completions) looks innocent — it should return apprentices who have completed nothing. But if any apprentice_id in completions is NULL, the entire query silently returns zero rows. Comparison with NULL is NULL, not TRUE, and the engine cannot prove the row is 'not in' the list. The bug is invisible — no error, just wrong data.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: The fix: NOT EXISTS never has the NULL problem. It just runs the inner subquery and asks 'did anything match?' — a yes-or-no answer, with no NULL ambiguity. Use NOT EXISTS by default. Use NOT IN only when the inner subquery is guaranteed NULL-free, and even then, future schema changes can introduce NULLs.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Trace the existence checks

Predict each query's result. Pay attention to NOT IN vs NOT EXISTS when NULLs are present.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a teammate why 'WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT apprentice_id FROM completions)' silently returns zero rows when even one row of completions has apprentice_id = NULL. Walk through the boolean evaluation.

options: The inner query references a column from the outer query, so it re-runs once per outer row
It uses the CORRELATE keyword
It is nested more than two levels deep
It is in the FROM clause rather than WHERE
questions.correctAnswer: The inner query references a column from the outer query, so it re-runs once per outer row
questions.explanationHtml: The dependence on an outer-row column is what makes it correlated. A regular (uncorrelated) subquery runs once and its result is reused for every outer row.

questions.questionHtml:
Using the four-apprentice / four-completion model, what does this query return?

SELECT a.name FROM apprentices a
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM completions c WHERE c.apprentice_id = a.id
);
options: Dorian
Alice, Bjorn, Cassia
All four apprentices
Nothing
questions.explanationHtml: NOT EXISTS keeps apprentices for whom the inner subquery finds zero matching rows. Alice, Bjorn, and Cassia each have completions; Dorian has none. So Dorian is the only result.

options: EXISTS only checks for the existence of any row, not the values, so the projection content is irrelevant — '1' is a convention signaling that
It is required by SQL syntax — only constants are allowed inside EXISTS
It improves performance by reducing the number of bytes transferred
It is the only way to use EXISTS without throwing an error
questions.correctAnswer: EXISTS only checks for the existence of any row, not the values, so the projection content is irrelevant — '1' is a convention signaling that
questions.explanationHtml: EXISTS evaluates to true if the subquery would return at least one row, regardless of what's in those rows. SELECT 1, SELECT *, SELECT NULL are all equivalent inside EXISTS. The convention SELECT 1 tells the next reader "the projection is intentionally a placeholder."

questions.questionHtml:
You see this query in production:

SELECT a.name FROM apprentices a
WHERE a.id NOT IN (SELECT apprentice_id FROM completions);

It quietly stops returning any rows, even though there are clearly apprentices with no completions. What's the most likely cause?
options: At least one row in completions has apprentice_id = NULL, so NOT IN evaluates to NULL (not TRUE) for every outer row
NOT IN is no longer supported in modern SQL engines
The completions table now uses an index that breaks NOT IN
apprentices was renamed and the query is silently joining wrong tables
questions.correctAnswer: At least one row in completions has apprentice_id = NULL, so NOT IN evaluates to NULL (not TRUE) for every outer row
questions.explanationHtml: This is the canonical NOT IN + NULL bug. x NOT IN (list with NULL) always evaluates to NULL because the engine cannot prove that x is unequal to NULL. The query "runs fine" but returns nothing. The fix is to switch to NOT EXISTS, which is immune to this trap.

subChunks.title: Common Table Expressions — WITH
subChunks.hookHtml: By the time a query has three nested subqueries, even careful readers get lost. Common Table Expressions (CTEs) — the WITH clause — let you name intermediate results and chain them, top to bottom. Same logic, dramatically clearer.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The shape of a CTE

WITH per_apprentice_xp AS (
  SELECT a.id, a.name, COALESCE(SUM(q.xp_reward), 0) AS earned
  FROM apprentices a
  LEFT JOIN completions c ON c.apprentice_id = a.id
  LEFT JOIN quests      q ON q.id = c.quest_id
  GROUP BY a.id, a.name
)
SELECT * FROM per_apprentice_xp
WHERE earned > 200
ORDER BY earned DESC;

The WITH name AS (...) defines a named, query-scoped intermediate result. The main query that follows can reference it by name as if it were a table. The CTE only exists for the duration of this one statement.

Multiple CTEs — chained

WITH per_apprentice AS (
  SELECT a.id, a.name, COUNT(c.id) AS num
  FROM apprentices a
  LEFT JOIN completions c ON c.apprentice_id = a.id
  GROUP BY a.id, a.name
),
threshold AS (
  SELECT AVG(num) AS avg_num FROM per_apprentice
)
SELECT name, num
FROM per_apprentice, threshold
WHERE per_apprentice.num > threshold.avg_num;

Comma-separated CTEs are evaluated top-down. Each one can reference any of the earlier ones — but not the later ones. The main SELECT at the bottom can reference all of them.

CTEs vs derived tables in FROM

The same logic, two ways to write it:

-- Derived table — denser, harder to follow:
SELECT name, num
FROM (
  SELECT a.id, a.name, COUNT(c.id) AS num
  FROM apprentices a
  LEFT JOIN completions c ON c.apprentice_id = a.id
  GROUP BY a.id, a.name
) per_apprentice
WHERE num > 1;

-- CTE — top-down, named, easier to follow:
WITH per_apprentice AS (
  SELECT a.id, a.name, COUNT(c.id) AS num
  FROM apprentices a
  LEFT JOIN completions c ON c.apprentice_id = a.id
  GROUP BY a.id, a.name
)
SELECT name, num FROM per_apprentice
WHERE num > 1;

For one intermediate step, derived tables are fine. For more than one, CTEs win on every metric — readability, debuggability (you can change the final SELECT to SELECT * FROM per_apprentice to inspect the intermediate result), and ease of reuse.

CTEs are query-scoped, not persisted

A CTE doesn't create a real table. It's a name that exists only for the duration of the surrounding statement. The next statement won't know what per_apprentice is. (Persistent equivalents — views and materialised views — are different features and not what we're discussing here.)

Performance — CTEs are not always free

In some engines (older PostgreSQL versions notably), CTEs were treated as optimisation fences — the engine had to materialise them before joining, even when inlining would have been faster. PostgreSQL 12+ inlines non-recursive CTEs by default. Modern MySQL, SQL Server, and SQLite generally inline. The lesson: don't avoid CTEs for performance reasons in modern engines, but if you're tuning a hot query and a CTE is involved, check the explain plan.

The full pipeline, with CTEs

WITH cte_1 AS ( ... ),
     cte_2 AS ( ... another query, possibly using cte_1 ... ),
     cte_3 AS ( ... )
SELECT ...
FROM cte_3
JOIN cte_2 ON ...
WHERE ...;

When you find yourself writing a query with two or more derived tables, or the same subquery twice, reach for CTEs. They are the single biggest readability tool in modern SQL.

storyBeats.text: Cipher unrolls a much longer scroll — three queries, each cleanly separated, building on each other.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Subqueries get unreadable past two levels of nesting. The fix is the WITH clause — Common Table Expressions, or CTEs. You name an intermediate result, then use that name in the main query. It's the SQL equivalent of breaking a long expression into named local variables in any other language.

storyBeats.speaker: From nested mess to clear pipeline
storyBeats.text:
-- Without CTE — possible, but already cluttered:
SELECT name, earned
FROM (
  SELECT a.id, a.name,
         COALESCE(SUM(q.xp_reward), 0) AS earned
  FROM apprentices a
  LEFT JOIN completions c ON c.apprentice_id = a.id
  LEFT JOIN quests      q ON q.id = c.quest_id
  GROUP BY a.id, a.name
) per_apprentice
WHERE earned > 200;

-- With CTE — top-down, named:
WITH per_apprentice_xp AS (
  SELECT a.id, a.name,
         COALESCE(SUM(q.xp_reward), 0) AS earned
  FROM apprentices a
  LEFT JOIN completions c ON c.apprentice_id = a.id
  LEFT JOIN quests      q ON q.id = c.quest_id
  GROUP BY a.id, a.name
)
SELECT name, earned
FROM per_apprentice_xp
WHERE earned > 200;

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: The biggest practical benefit of CTEs is debuggability. If your final query returns wrong numbers, you can change the bottom SELECT name, earned FROM per_apprentice_xp WHERE earned > 200 to SELECT * FROM per_apprentice_xp and inspect the intermediate result. The pipeline is split into named stages you can probe one at a time. With deeply nested subqueries you cannot do that without surgery.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: And you can chain them — comma-separated, evaluated top-down. WITH cte_1 AS (...), cte_2 AS (... can read cte_1 ...), cte_3 AS (... reads either ...) SELECT .... Each CTE has access to all the earlier ones. The main query can read all of them. This is how complex reports are written in production — never one giant nested query, but a stack of named CTEs each with one clear job.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Trace the CTE pipelines

For each query, identify each CTE's purpose, then how the main SELECT uses them.
subChunks.guidedPracticeStarterCode:
-- apprentices: Alice(1, 1200), Bjorn(2, 2400), Cassia(3, 4800), Dorian(4, 80)
-- quests:      1=Tame the Slime(100), 2=Decode the Glyph(180),
--              3=Forge the Blade(400)
-- completions: (app=1,q=1), (app=2,q=1), (app=2,q=2), (app=3,q=3)

-- Query A — single CTE:
WITH per_apprentice_xp AS (
  SELECT a.id, a.name,
         COALESCE(SUM(q.xp_reward), 0) AS earned
  FROM apprentices a
  LEFT JOIN completions c ON c.apprentice_id = a.id
  LEFT JOIN quests      q ON q.id = c.quest_id
  GROUP BY a.id, a.name
)
SELECT name, earned FROM per_apprentice_xp
ORDER BY earned DESC;

-- Query B — chained CTEs:
WITH per_apprentice AS (
  SELECT a.id, a.name, COUNT(c.id) AS num_done
  FROM apprentices a
  LEFT JOIN completions c ON c.apprentice_id = a.id
  GROUP BY a.id, a.name
),
threshold AS (
  SELECT AVG(num_done) AS avg_done FROM per_apprentice
)
SELECT p.name, p.num_done
FROM per_apprentice p, threshold t
WHERE p.num_done > t.avg_done;

-- Query C — CTE for clarity, with a final WHERE:
WITH active AS (
  SELECT a.id, a.name
  FROM apprentices a
  WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM completions c WHERE c.apprentice_id = a.id)
)
SELECT * FROM active
ORDER BY name;
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would refactor a query with two or three nested subqueries into a single WITH ... statement. Give one concrete debuggability win that CTEs offer over derived tables in FROM.

options: A named, query-scoped intermediate result defined with WITH; usable in the main query as if it were a table
A persistent denormalised table, refreshed on a schedule
A type of index optimised for joins
An alias for a single column
questions.correctAnswer: A named, query-scoped intermediate result defined with WITH; usable in the main query as if it were a table
questions.explanationHtml: CTEs give a name to a SELECT and then reuse it in the surrounding statement. They exist only for the duration of the statement — they don't create a persistent table. Persistent denormalised tables are called materialised views in PostgreSQL.

questions.questionHtml:
Using the four-apprentice model with completion counts (Alice=1, Bjorn=2, Cassia=1, Dorian=0; average = 1.0), what does this query return?

WITH per_apprentice AS (
  SELECT a.id, a.name, COUNT(c.id) AS num
  FROM apprentices a
  LEFT JOIN completions c ON c.apprentice_id = a.id
  GROUP BY a.id, a.name
),
threshold AS (
  SELECT AVG(num) AS avg_num FROM per_apprentice
)
SELECT p.name, p.num
FROM per_apprentice p, threshold t
WHERE p.num > t.avg_num;
options: Bjorn, 2
Alice, Bjorn, Cassia
Bjorn
Nobody — average equals every count
questions.explanationHtml: Only Bjorn has more than the average (1.0). Alice and Cassia have exactly 1; Dorian has 0. p.num > t.avg_num is strictly greater, so only Bjorn qualifies. The result includes Bjorn's count (2) because the main SELECT projects both name and num.

questions.questionHtml: What is the cleanest way to chain three intermediate computations in one query?
options: Three CTEs separated by commas, evaluated top-down: WITH a AS (...), b AS (...), c AS (...) SELECT ...
Three nested derived tables in FROM
Three separate queries, with the result of each pasted into the next
A single deeply-nested subquery in WHERE
questions.correctAnswer: Three CTEs separated by commas, evaluated top-down: WITH a AS (...), b AS (...), c AS (...) SELECT ...
questions.explanationHtml: Comma-chained CTEs read top-to-bottom like a small pipeline. Each step has a name; later steps can refer to earlier ones. This is the production-default for any non-trivial reporting query.

questions.questionHtml: A junior writes a deeply-nested 3-subquery report and asks if they should refactor it as CTEs. What's the strongest argument for the refactor?
options: Each CTE can be named and inspected independently — change the final SELECT to SELECT * FROM cte_2 to debug the middle stage
CTEs are always faster than nested subqueries
CTEs persist across statements like temporary tables
Nested subqueries are deprecated in modern SQL
questions.correctAnswer: Each CTE can be named and inspected independently — change the final SELECT to SELECT * FROM cte_2 to debug the middle stage
questions.explanationHtml: Debuggability is the killer app for CTEs. With nested subqueries, isolating one stage means surgery — replacing the outer query, fiddling with brackets. With CTEs, you change the bottom SELECT and inspect any intermediate result. Performance-wise, CTEs and nested subqueries are usually optimised to the same plan in modern engines. CTEs do NOT persist across statements (that's views) and nested subqueries are not deprecated.
